lecture_summary: The lecture introduces rotational kinematics as the circular-motion analogue of translational kinematics: θ↔x, ω↔v, and α↔a; s=rθ, v=rω, and a_t=rα; radial versus tangential acceleration; and constant-angular-acceleration equations. Its representative example finds when a disk with ω(t)=a−bt² reverses direction and integrates ω(t) to obtain angular displacement, emphasizing that variable acceleration requires calculus. The broader problem-solving message is to model the system, state assumptions, choose representations, test equation applicability, and only then calculate.

No video explicitly matches the representative function ω(t)=a−bt², finding reversal from ω=0, and integrating it to obtain 72 rad; the selected videos collectively cover the required method.
The playlist descriptions do not show a strong focused treatment of radians, rotational sign conventions, or formal radial–tangential unit-vector notation.
The torque and angular-momentum equations are only brief previews in this lecture, so dedicated later-topic videos were excluded to keep the set minimal.
